question: How tall is the Sagrada Família's central tower, and what does it represent?

Sagrada Família. Location: Eixample district, Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain. Architect: Antoni Gaudí (took over from Francisco de Paula del Villar after Villar's resignation on 18 March 1883 due to disagreements with the construction board; Gaudí was formally appointed Architect Director on 28 March 1884 and redesigned the project, keeping only the crypt). Style: Gothic Revival combined with curvilinear Art Nouveau / Catalan Modernisme. Status: Still under construction. On 30 October 2025 it became the tallest church building in the world, surpassing Ulm Minster (161.5 m); it reached its full height of 172.5 m on 20 February 2026. The main structure was targeted for completion around 2026 (the centenary of Gaudí's death), but sculptural details, decoration, and a planned monumental stairway are expected to continue until 2034. Funded solely by private donations and visitor entry fees, with no government or church funding. Received 3 million visitors by 1990 and 5 million in 2025.. UNESCO: The Nativity façade and Crypt were added to the existing (1984) 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' UNESCO World Heritage Site listing in 2005.
answer: The central tower of the Sagrada Família is 172.5 meters tall, surpassing the Ulm Minster as the tallest church building in the world. It represents the central figure of the church's design, symbolizing the central nave and the spiritual heart of the building.

Symbolic references throughout include political Catalanism (entrance stairway) and Catholicism (the Calvary, originally conceived as a chapel). question: Name two specific structures, in two different Gaudí projects, that use catenary or inverted-catenary arches, and explain what problem this technique solves.
reference: Examples include the elevated viaducts at Park Güell, whose columns use inverted catenary arches for load-bearing, and the loft of Casa Batlló, whose sixty catenary arches form a ribcage-like structure. The catenary distributes weight evenly, affected only by self-cancelling tangential forces, letting Gaudí support loads without buttresses.
contexts: Viaducts / elevated pathways (part of park_guell). Materials: local stone. As with Gaudí's earlier work at Colònia Güell, the viaducts use inverted catenary arches to achieve optimal load-bearing compression, so the stone columns work in pure compression without needing external buttressing. Columns and vaulted supports mimic tree trunks and natural forms, part of Gaudí's naturalist-period design language for the park.

answer: In Antoni Gaudí's Park Güell, the network of elevated stone pathways and viaducts uses inclined columns of local stone to mimic tree trunks and inverted catenary arches for load-bearing compression. question: How does dragon imagery connect Casa Batlló, Park Güell, and Gaudí's Catalan identity?

Park Güell (part of Park Güell). Materials: local stone (viaducts and columns), trencadís (broken tile/ceramic mosaic). Inspired by the English garden-city movement (hence the English word 'Park' in its name); marks Gaudí's 'naturalist period', in which his study of nature and organic forms drove both ornament and underlying structural geometry. Symbolic references throughout include political Catalanism (entrance stairway) and Catholicism (the Calvary, originally conceived as a chapel). Uses inverted catenary arches for its viaducts and elevated pathways, the same load-bearing-compression method Gaudí used earlier at Colònia Güell. Entry to the Monumental Zone (main terrace, mosaics, viaducts, gate area) has required a paid ticket since October 2013; Barcelona residents enter free. UNESCO's 1984 inscription describes the park's architecture as combining the Arts and Crafts movement, Symbolism, Expressionism, and Rationalism, and as having presaged techniques of 20th-century Modernism. Introduced curved, undulating benches at Park Güell -- a precursor to the style Gaudí later fully realized at the Sagrada Família.

answer: Dragon imagery connects Casa Batlló, Park Güell, and Gaudí's Catalan identity through its association with Saint George, the patron saint of Catalonia.
